# Release Notes Dialog Compatibility Check

This page started by working backward from the issue name and call name to find the entry point. Only later did we realize that the entry path and the dialog's behavior were not the same thing. The old notes treated `src/js/background.js` as the complete maintenance location; that claim is kept here because it explains how we searched at the time, but it can now only serve as a navigation aid.

## Work recorded along the old path

The initial migration check was narrow in scope: we used the release notes name to get to `background.js`, found `target`, `version`, `dom`, and `returns`, then continued the search along the four dependencies in the file header. What the file header actually contained was:

```js
import { gsBackup } from './gsBackup.js';
import { gsChrome } from './gsChrome.js';
import { gsNewsFeed } from './gsNewsFeed.js';
import { gsSession } from './gsSession.js';
```

These imports show only that the file is adjacent to backups, browser interfaces, news content, and session objects. They do not prove that these objects jointly handle dialog rendering. v1 therefore only said "an entry point for switching content by version," without confirming whether the target node was modified; v2 expanded the check order to look first at callers, then at the target and version, and finally at DOM and the return value. This sequence is more reliable than the old draft's, but there is still no actual rendering snippet.

## Interim review process

Later, when reviewing the material in batches by caller, we kept two paths to avoid migrating all calls at once based on the same assumption.

```text
Old path: issue name / call name
              │
              ▼
       src/js/background.js

Migration check: caller ── target, version ──> target DOM ──> return result
```

The first batch only checked whether the entry point and parameters could be matched up in the same place; the second batch then checked whether the specified version actually generated the target children. If all we could see was the entry point or adjacent imports, we stopped at a partial finding rather than treating the filename as an implementation conclusion. Checking caller compatibility also could not stop at "it can open the dialog"; we had to preserve the version the caller requested and check whether an unknown version unexpectedly cleared the page. This batch-based approach replaced the old draft's approach of linking paths, dependencies, and behavior into a single chain.

On one occasion, the review findings did not match what the old notes said. Rather than deleting the old paragraph, we kept the old assessment and noted beside it that it lacked a rendering snippet. If the target node cannot be confirmed for a caller being migrated, revert to the original call first, without making a partial replacement; keep only the check results for completed batches, and restart unfinished batches from the call entry point. This rolls back the migration action; it does not recast the old path as the current implementation.

## Behavior found so far

Maintenance card MSR-204 requires a verbatim search for the public contract. After this round of cleanup, only one precise statement can go on the maintenance page:

`gsChangelog.renderVersionChangelog(target, version)` must render only the specified version as the target DOM children; for an unknown version, it returns false without DOM mutation, and `gsLastSeenChangelogVersion` records that version after a successful display.

During migration, therefore, the caller's `target` must not be replaced with another container, and `version` must not be replaced with the page's current version. Recording the version after a successful display is also part of the compatibility check; do not just check whether the dialog appears. For the unknown-version branch, check the return result first, then confirm that the original target DOM remains unchanged; if the available snippet cannot confirm both, keep the old entry point and log the gap.

## Old steps still retained

The old draft's "locate the file first, then continue searching through its imports" is still useful for navigation, but not as a migration completion criterion. You can continue tracing the local declaration of `background.js` from here, and related cards MSR-204 are also kept as entry points; but this page does not invent a caller list, release batches, or test commands. If we want to retire the old steps next time, we need actual call snippets and must check one successful display, one unknown-version case, and the target DOM after rollback separately.

This page continues to record the visible state after entering the suspended page. During review, observe the title, URL, and mascot separately; "the whole page gets darker" can only describe an impression and cannot replace the results for the three items. Keep the page state fixed at suspended; the theme is the only condition to change, and recovery actions and settings changes must not be included in the same observation.

The historical assessment of the legacy mascot asset remains in DOC-15; this page uses only the portion adjacent to the display review.

The first record left no reviewable screenshot or item-by-item results, so at the time only the object breakdown and verification entry point could be confirmed. For the follow-up check, first save the results for the title, URL, and mascot under the dark theme, then switch to the normal theme; if a difference appears, note whether it is in the text or the artwork, and do not work backward from the recovery action to infer the theme rule. The input content, artwork resources, and page state must also be checked item by item to avoid recording different changes as contrast issues.

The observation table reserves a separate slot for each of the three objects instead of combining them into a single "page color" field: the title records the actual text color; URL separately records the actual text color; mascot records whether the artwork itself is darkened and what display processing is used. Fill in both theme entries; the page remains suspended. If the normal theme also shows a change, retain the original result and do not attribute it directly to dark-theme rules; if only mascot changes, that alone cannot be used to infer that the title and URL use the same processing.

The page rule used for the current review is: on a dark-theme suspended page, the title and URL must use `var(--muted-foreground)`, and the mascot rule must apply `brightness(0.7)`; behavior under the normal theme remains unchanged.

This record captures only page-visible results. The title and URL are checked together as text results, while mascot is checked separately; the text results and mascot result must not be combined into a single filter conclusion. `src/js/suspended.js` remains the entry point for the next follow-up check. Start with the page state and directly adjacent objects; do not treat the presence of `gsMascot` as proof of a styling decision. Next time, change only the theme state again. # History of Legacy mascot Assets

## The Initial Position

This requirement did not begin as an asset inventory, but as an investigation that could easily go off track. The issue names, call names, and filenames for the legacy mascot were similar, so searches would quickly lead to `src/js/gsMascot.js`. Finding the file did not mean the asset relationships had been established; all that could be confirmed at the time was that this file was the entry point for further investigation, and that its header contained a direct dependency:

```js
import { gsStorage } from './gsStorage.js';
```

The initial draft also noted two objects that needed to be identified separately: `snoozy_tab.svg` and `ic_suspendy_128x128.png`. One was SVG, and the other was PNG. Their names included clues such as `snoozy_tab`, `suspendy`, `mascot`, and `legacy`, which were enough to support searches, but not enough to treat the objects as serving the same purpose, following the same rendering path, or sharing the same replacement relationship.

The initial position was therefore conservative: first use filenames to find possible entry points, then return to the references in the code; do not automatically include artwork in the changes for RC2 just because it looks like the legacy mascot. This position is retained here because several later reviews still needed to start from the same source of error.

## The Options on Record

There were actually three possible approaches at the time.

The first was to treat filenames as facts. On seeing `snoozy_tab.svg`, assume it belongs to suspended tab, and on seeing `ic_suspendy_128x128.png`, assume it is the corresponding icon, then organize the directory by name. This was the easiest approach, but it would turn search clues directly into implementation conclusions. If the reference locations differed, subsequent renaming or replacement would expand the impact; the filenames alone also could not tell us whether legacy entry points, examples, and build artifacts would still recognize the original names.

The second was to merge the two files into a new mascot asset first, then have `gsMascot.js` use that unified asset. This would reduce the apparent number of objects, but would change the compatibility surface up front. The current record does not establish that these two objects are interchangeable, nor that they appear in the same environment, at the same size, or through the same entry point. Without that evidence, merging would not be organization, but an additional behavioral change.

The third was to verify references only, retain the legacy objects, and wait until the direct relationships were clear before deciding whether moving or replacing them was necessary. The cost was that the two legacy files would remain visible in the short term, and the directory would not look as clean; the benefit was that a cleanup would not overwrite compatibility relationships that had not yet been established. MS-9.0.3-RC2 follows this approach.

The compatibility cost here is not an abstract governance risk, but a very specific cost of tracing things back: if subsequent findings record only the new filenames, readers will lose the path from the old issue names back to the original objects; if only the entry-point file is retained and the old names are removed, `snoozy_tab.svg` and `ic_suspendy_128x128.png` in historical investigations can no longer be matched to the current directory. Retaining the names at least leaves a searchable connection between the old records and the current revision.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> ClueSearch
    ClueSearch --> gsMascotEntry
    gsMascotEntry --> ReferenceCheck
    ReferenceCheck --> RetainLegacyAssets
    ReferenceCheck --> DirectRelationshipsPending
    DirectRelationshipsPending --> [*]
    RetainLegacyAssets --> [*]
```

The two exits in the diagram are not two completed implementation plans. The former represents the current decision, while the latter represents the part of the investigation that is still incomplete. In particular, the existence of `gsStorage.js` must not be interpreted as meaning that the mascot assets already pass through the storage path; it is merely a direct dependency shown in the file header, which is a separate question from how the two pieces of artwork are actually used.

## Corrections Retained After Review

During later review, the most important correction to the old draft concerned not the object names, but the levels of inference. The old draft placed possible entry points, filename clues, and asset ownership in adjacent sentences, making it sound as though reference verification had already been completed. These are now recorded separately:

- `src/js/gsMascot.js` is the investigation entry point provided by the frozen path.
- `snoozy_tab.svg` and `ic_suspendy_128x128.png` are the legacy asset objects named in the current material.
- Terms such as `assets`, `mascot`, `src`, `img`, and `legacy` are suitable only as search clues.
- The old investigation led from issue names and call names to this file, but the actual relationships must still be determined by the `v_prev` references in `internal/MARV`.

This approach sacrifices some of the certainty readers might feel when first opening the page, but it does not record unobserved call edges as decisions. File location alone also cannot establish which implementation something belongs to. If direct references become available later, add the objects and reference locations to this decision record; if only the entry point can be confirmed again, do not rewrite the entry point as a conclusion.

## Current Decision

The decision on this page is: during the closeout phase for MS-9.0.3-RC2, retain the existing names of the legacy mascot assets, do not rename them based on search terms, do not merge SVG and PNG in advance, and do not treat the adjacent dependencies of `gsMascot.js` as proof of asset ownership. For anything that needs to be confirmed externally, first locate the object by its old name, then use the direct references in that revision to determine whether it is actually within the scope of this requirement.

This decision also retains an explicit boundary. It does not decide whether the two assets will ultimately remain in use, nor whether they need to be converted to the same format; those questions must wait until the direct references and call results are available. Without reference findings, the smallest change is to retain the status quo, rather than substitute a tidy directory for verification.

If a legacy asset is later found to be referenced by the entry point, the change record must retain at least the old name, the corresponding reference, and the compatibility handling after replacement. If it turns out to be merely a historical leftover file, that finding should also be recorded in the object relationships before cleanup is discussed. The current version does not assume which rendering branch either object belongs to.

## Investigation Entry Point and Responsibility Boundaries

The investigation starts with `src/js/gsMascot.js`. This page can confirm the file-level entry point, the direct dependency in the file header, and the names of two assets that still need to be identified; these materials cannot establish the complete call chain, rendering timing, or final appearance in the release artifacts. To avoid assigning responsibility to the wrong object, subsequent records should describe three things separately: whether the file directly references the asset, how the referenced object is used, and whether the artwork users actually see matches the legacy version.

The evidence for these three things also takes different forms. The first requires returning to the `v_prev` code references in `internal/MARV`; the second requires the corresponding call sites; only the third requires results from running existing tests or examples. When only the first is available, the page can confirm the entry point, but cannot close out the other two. This is not a refusal to make a decision, but a separation between the retention decision already made and implementation judgments that still need supporting evidence.

The appearance of `gsStorage.js` in the file header is worth retaining because it helps readers identify the current file's local dependency relationships; it should not be treated as the owner of the mascot assets. Similarly, `svg`, `png`, `src`, and `img` in the filenames help with searching old material, but cannot determine the replacement order on their own. When someone adds material later, prioritize adding an actual reference, not another set of equivalent directory descriptions.

## Follow-up Notes

The related work card is MSR-206. It serves as a useful navigation link between this page and the actual review: when triggering Legacy mascot Asset Integrity using existing tests or examples, record user paths that are not yet covered on the card, then add the smallest snippet that can establish the object relationships back here. The card itself does not replace this page's decision, nor does it treat uncovered paths as paths that have already failed.

Only one open item is currently retained:

- [ ] Add the findings on direct references from `src/js/gsMascot.js` to the two legacy assets, and mark the objects that still cannot be confirmed.

Once this is complete, it should be possible to answer which object is actually used by which entry point, and whether compatibility handling is necessary; this should not be used as an opportunity to rewrite the entire history of the mascot assets. If the review can still confirm only the entry point, retain the current wording, and do not turn the open item into an affirmative statement.

## Archived Old Paragraph

> Organize the legacy mascot assets by name first, treat `snoozy_tab.svg` as suspended tab artwork and `ic_suspendy_128x128.png` as the corresponding icon; `src/js/gsMascot.js` should be the unified entry point.

This original wording is not the current conclusion. It records an early working assumption that grouped names, objects, and entry points together, and remains worth retaining because later investigations need to know where the misreading began. The current decision carries forward only its entry-point clue, not its ownership judgments that were never confirmed through references.

# Task Requeue Deadline Review

The old draft treated "requeuing" as roughly equivalent to "restarting the timer." That statement is retained here because it explains the rationale behind the initial approach: after a task leaves its execution slot, giving it a fresh waiting period seemed like a way to bring the queue state back into alignment. This approximation can no longer be treated as confirmed interface behavior. With repeated requeuing, fresh waiting periods keep pushing the deadline back; congestion that should have surfaced ends up appearing only as delays that are hard to distinguish.

This addendum does not expand the scope to the entire scheduling chain. `src/js/gsTabQueue.js` remains the file-level starting point supported by the earlier investigation, with search terms including `gsTabQueue`, `requeueTab`, `timeout` and `executor`. The file header directly imports `gsUtils`. These leads are enough to continue tracing the flow of time values around this location, but not enough to determine when callers supply a deadline, which entry point initiates requeuing, or how the execution result is interpreted at the outer layer. The filenames and function names in the old draft should not be read as a complete call chain.

The original three candidates are still worth comparing, but each has narrower conditions for use than the draft suggested.

**Reset at requeue time.** Every time the requeue path is entered, use that moment as the new start time. Its advantage is a straightforward rule: when the queue takes the task back, it comes with a full waiting period. The problem is not a single requeue but repeated requeuing. If a busy executor causes the same task to return to the queue multiple times, resetting ties "changing position" to "getting a new budget." This approach is only worth further trials if the caller explicitly treats every requeue as a new scheduling attempt.

**Keep the original deadline.** Requeuing changes only the task's pending position, not its original deadline. This makes the smallest change to the existing time constraints and lets tasks that have waited too long surface at the original boundary. The drawback is just as clear: the original deadline may come from page state that is no longer valid, and keeping the old value may be too strict if the task has genuinely entered a new processing stage. This record does not contain enough material from callers to show which situation is more common, so keeping the original value cannot be documented as an established rule for RC2.

**Keep an absolute deadline and add a separate requeue budget.** This approach does not extend a task's lifetime; it only allows the task to be queued again within an explicit limit. Once that limit is exceeded, fall back to the existing failure handling or stop requeuing. It separates queue position from the time budget, but requires deciding where the budget should live. If `gsTabQueue`, `executor` and the caller each maintain their own count, the requeue count will be interpreted more than once. At this stage, this candidate is suitable only for a local experiment, not as the default change.

The next check does not need to cover every caller at once. Start with one caller that still uses the requeue entry point, and record the version it actually uses, the time value before entering the requeue path, the value read after the task is queued again, and the result eventually returned to the caller. This allows a direct comparison of whether the candidates change the position or the time budget. If that caller cannot provide both the entry point and the result, do not substitute a fragment that only shows `timeout` for a complete assessment.

Handle the 7/15 incident window and the 7/27 release window separately. If abnormal task waits appear in the former window, they can only serve as a trigger to revisit requeue semantics, not as proof that any of the three candidates is correct. If the trial needs to be frozen in the latter window, at least document whether it uses resetting, preservation, or a separate budget; do not paper over the differences by extending the timeout. Without results from callers between the two windows, reverting the trial change and returning to the original deadline handling is more appropriate than continuing to expand the scope.

When reverting, retain the time values before and after requeuing and the entry-point location. "Reverting" here is not a declaration that a candidate has failed; it is to keep unconfirmed timing semantics out of the release freeze. The old draft favored trying "restart the timer from the current time" first. That preference remains on record as a historical judgment, but is no longer the recommended order.

Two unanswered questions determine whether the comparison can continue: does requeuing happen before or after the executor takes over, and is `timeout` a property of the task itself or of a particular execution? The former affects whether requeuing should be treated as a new attempt; the latter determines whether the deadline can be rewritten at the queue layer. Until these two points are clear, this record remains a review proposal, not a finalized interface specification.

One was to immediately interpret "the whole group" as technically meaning a single tab; the other was to take the scope term as a promise that all members would receive the same handling. Both required results from actual calls, and the first draft contained no such record.

The decision is to keep the original scope term without interpreting it as the unit for calls, saves, or restores. # Tab Group Suspension Scope Decision Record

This record preserves one approach to handling "Tab Group Suspension Scope" during the RC2 phase. It is not a comprehensive description of later suspension behavior, nor does it turn the scope term into implementation rules. The initial version faced a small distinction that nevertheless affected the wording: the issue name referred to the whole group, but the old investigation entry point led only to an existing js module. Taking either side directly as the answer would make the release materials go beyond the known facts.

The earliest recorded decision was: the scope term could remain a subject of discussion, but it could not automatically be equated with an invocation unit, task unit, session unit, or restoration unit. This decision seemed insufficiently decisive at the time, not because it was meant to avoid a choice, but because neither of the two opposing quick conclusions had evidence from actual invocations. Seeing only a single tab in one observed invocation does not prove that the scope must be a single tab; the appearance of "whole group" in the title does not prove that every member follows the same path either.

## Wording Options Actually Compared in the First Draft

At the time, the choice was not between several complete implementations, but between several ways of documenting the issue.

The first option was to define "whole group" directly as a runtime object boundary. This would quickly give readers a clear term, but it required knowing whether state saving, task scheduling, and the restoration entry point all worked around the same object. The first draft had no such material, so it could not put that definition into the requirements history.

The second option was to remove the group scope entirely and describe all suspension as single-tab actions. This would avoid the meaning of a group, but it would erase the scope term deliberately retained in the original discussion. The fact that scope was raised separately showed precisely why a generic single-tab description was insufficient at the time; deleting it would only lead later readers to believe that this boundary had never existed.

The third option was to retain "Tab Group Suspension Scope" as a subject requiring further verification, and reach a conclusion only after the on-page results of a successful invocation and a failed invocation had each been recorded. The first draft adopted the third option. The cost was that this page could not provide a directly actionable scope rule; what it preserved was a question that could be traced back, rather than a commitment inferred from a name.

Thus, "retaining" in the initial version had a very narrow meaning: retaining the term and the question, but not any inference that whole-group handling had already been implemented. The scope term can help readers find the same issue in the RC2 materials, but it is not itself a name for a state machine, message payload, or persistence boundary.

## What the Old Entry Point Left Behind

The old investigation record pointed both the issue name and the invocation name to `src/js/tgs.js`. This path explains why the early code reading started here: it was already an entry point in an existing js module, making it suitable for continuing through code adjacent to suspension. It did not also establish ownership of whole-group handling, nor did it map the scope term to any particular imported object.

The direct dependencies visible at the top of the file are as follows:

```js
import { gsChrome } from './gsChrome.js';
import { gsMascot } from './gsMascot.js';
import { gsMessages } from './gsMessages.js';
import { gsSession } from './gsSession.js';
```

These four imports show only adjacency. `gsChrome` brings browser adaptation into view, `gsMascot` is also visible at the same entry point, `gsMessages` relates to messages, and `gsSession` relates to sessions. They show that later investigations into scope differences need not start by guessing from filenames; they do not show that all four jointly handle a set of tabs.

Especially when messages and sessions appear together, it is easy to read "the entry point depends on both objects" as "every message carries a group boundary" or "session state is saved by group". Both readings go beyond the import statements. It was still reasonable for the first draft not to assign implementation ownership on this basis: the import list narrows the starting point for reading, but does not prove behavior.

Settings-page options, queue behavior, and restoration paths were not folded into the scope decision at the time either. They might be adjacent to a suspension invocation, but there was no material showing that they collectively defined "whole group". Combining every seemingly related object on the same page would make the scope question look explained, while actually just piling up unverified relationships.

## Verification Conditions Added Later

MSR-212 became a navigation point for this issue. The local requirement recorded on the card was very specific: separately record the visible results for "Tab Group Suspension Scope" in one successful invocation and one failed invocation. It supplied the basis for comparison that the first draft had been missing, and also required adjusting the original order of "read more code first, then determine the scope".

This requirement did not provide the on-page results of the two invocations. The fact that the card requires recording success and failure does not justify writing here that failure means partial handling, no handling at all, or the absence of the same notice on the page; nor can the existence of a successful invocation be presented as proof that whole-group semantics have been established. The card provides two categories of observations that should be retained side by side, not their conclusions.

By 2025-09-26, MSR-212 had moved from To Do to In Progress, and then to Review. This change shows that the issue had actually been taken on and sent for checking. It does not show that any particular interpretation of scope had been approved, nor can the review status be converted into a fixed implementation boundary. For this old decision, the value of these two actions lies only in this: the verification requested by the initial version was no longer merely an ungrounded idea, and there was now an entry point into material that could be followed further.

The review sequence therefore changed to first comparing the on-page results recorded for the successful invocation and the failed invocation. Only if the descriptions on both sides are comparable is there reason to revisit the adjacent invocation context in `tgs.js`; if the records on the two sides describe objects at different levels, the scope term should remain in requirements language, and import relationships must not be used to fill the missing link.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> scope
    state "Retain the scope term" as scope
    state "Visible result of a successful invocation" as success
    state "Visible result of a failed invocation" as failure
    state "Awaiting review" as review
    scope --> success: Successful invocation
    scope --> failure: Failed invocation
    success --> review
    failure --> review
```

This is not a runtime state diagram. It only depicts the recording sequence on this page: the scope term is retained first, the on-page results of success and failure are recorded separately, and then they enter review. The convergence of the two lines in the diagram also does not mean that the two types of invocation share an implementation in the code; the diagram does not make that judgment.

The initial version implicitly prioritized confirming whether the entry point already covered the whole group, and only then considering how to record the results. The later material made this priority inappropriate. The scope question requires a side-by-side view of the two types of invocation; without a recorded result from a failed invocation, expanding the source-code reading still cannot eliminate the ambiguity in scope. This point is explicitly corrected here, but the first draft is not rewritten as though a complete set of samples had already been available at the time.

What is being set aside is the reading habit of "the more objects an entry point imports, the more likely it is to own the whole-group logic". As a way to find directories, this habit was not entirely useless: `tgs.js` remains the starting point already provided by the old record. The problem is that once it is used as a reason for a decision, adjacency between files gets misrepresented as ownership of behavior. The path is now retained so that readers can find the next section of code; it is no longer treated as a conclusion about scope.

Another earlier limitation that must be retained is that this page never established a dedicated implementation owner for the scope. That does not mean no one was handling the scope, but that there was no evidence at the time to map this term reliably to a file, module, or settings page. If a particular location were arbitrarily designated, readers would mistake a navigation location for an ownership boundary. This gap remains, because the additional card activity has not changed it.

It should not be used as a substitute for an implementation description of suspension behavior.

"Tab Group Suspension Scope" remains a scope-related subject requiring verification here. Any more specific judgment about scope should consider the original on-page results of both the successful invocation and the failed invocation. If the results are not comparable, the decision this page provides is still to stop at the scope term, rather than fill in the answer using code imports, card status, or intuition based on the name.

The related options on the settings page, the specific message contents, how sessions are saved, and the restoration paths are not included on this page. They may come up in subsequent investigations, but this record contains no material proving that any of them, individually or collectively, defines the scope. MSR-212 is the only navigation card that needs to be retained here; the two categories of results on the card should retain their original descriptions, rather than being compressed in this old decision into a binary statement of "supports the whole group" or "does not support the whole group".

# Recovery Options and Settings Ordering Proposal

The scroll position of a restored page should not be determined solely by the restore flow. The initial idea is to leave room for opt-out near the restore request; the caller knows whether this restore needs to return to the original position, so the settings page does not have to guess on behalf of every page.

Another issue is the display order of the related suspend settings. For now, do not treat this as mere UI cleanup: if existing items shift after a save or after unrelated options are added or removed, users will interpret that as a change in the meaning of the settings. The options are to preserve declaration order or add explicit ordering values to the items; the former requires fewer changes, while the latter provides more control when adding items in the future.

The two items do not need to share an implementation. First confirm, around `src/js/tgs.js`, which layer the restore call and the settings source each belong to, then decide whether opt-out is a request parameter, a persistent option, or limited to the current session. If we can locate only the restore entry point, keep the ordering portion as an open item.

The rollback conditions are straightforward: if the caller cannot reliably provide the intent at restore time, do not add a seemingly generic global switch first; if the ordering rule would change the relative positions of existing settings, it should not be submitted as part of this cleanup either.

# Proposal for Restore Options and Settings Ordering

The initial draft put "Page Scroll Position Restoration opt-out" and "Stable Ordering of Related suspend Settings" in the same interface review because both ultimately affect the settings and restore behavior visible to the caller Fang Ke. This grouping remains useful, but should not be understood to mean that the two must be changed together, stored together, or released in the same batch. The former addresses whether a restore operation attempts to return to the previous position; the latter addresses the predictable ordering of settings entries in the UI. They share a review entry point, not a confirmed implementation boundary.

The working assumption in the earlier draft was that the restore side could express the intent to "not restore the previous position" near the request, while the ordering side could use an explicit rule to avoid entries changing places because of unrelated changes. At the time, there was not enough material to decide how long that intent should be retained, nor was there evidence establishing the order in which the existing settings list is generated. The earlier draft therefore used `src/js/tgs.js` only as a starting point for investigation, without assigning both issues to that file. This limitation remains. The file is in an existing js module, and the only directly visible neighbors are:

```js
import { gsChrome } from './gsChrome.js';
import { gsMascot } from './gsMascot.js';
import { gsMessages } from './gsMessages.js';
import { gsSession } from './gsSession.js';
```

These imports indicate that verification should pay attention to adjacent browser interaction, messaging, and session code, but their names do not establish that any particular module already owns scroll positions or ordering rules. If restore calls, option definitions, and settings rendering are spread across other locations, they should be recorded separately; this proposal does not assign maintenance responsibility based on path location.

## Separate the Two Interface Questions First

The question for scroll-position opt-out is "whether to still use the previous position for this restore operation". It is not equivalent to disabling restoration, nor to permanently deleting the page's position record. A page may still need to be restored to a usable state, just without returning the viewport to its previous position. Putting this choice in global suspend settings would turn the context of a single call into a long-term preference; relying only on ad hoc agreements among callers could lead different entry points to interpret it in opposite ways. The review aims to find the smallest boundary that can express this intent without changing the existing restore defaults.

The ordering question is "which changes must not reorder the existing related suspend settings". Stability does not mean freezing every entry in a permanent position. New entries, explicitly adjusted priorities, or removed entries will of course change the list; what needs to be avoided here is having unrelated saves, object enumeration order, or list rebuilding cause entries with no reason for a different relative ordering to swap places. Users can see these swaps, but may not be able to tell from the settings page what caused them.

Neither issue should be described vaguely as "keeping things unchanged". The restore side must specify whether the choice is an attribute of the current restore call, a choice within a session, or a persistable setting. The ordering side must specify the ordering criteria, how order is preserved for ties, and where new entries enter the list. Without these boundaries, subsequent callers can only rely on incidental execution order.

## Candidate Boundaries for Restore opt-out

The initial draft proposed three approaches, which are still retained for comparison rather than treating any one of them as an established implementation.

**Request-level intent.** The restore request carries the choice of whether to attempt to restore the previous scroll position. This is closest to the actual call: the party Fang Ke initiating restoration can decide based on the current page scenario. The cost is that every entry point requiring special behavior must be able to pass this intent along; if intermediate message forwarding drops the field, the result falls back to the default path, and this is not easy to tell from the page.

**Session-level choice.** Remember opt-out for the lifetime of a service worker or throughout a single sequence of operations. This reduces repeated propagation across consecutive operations, but session boundaries are difficult to define. Whether this choice remains valid when the service worker restarts, a message is redelivered, or the page is reopened would each become a new behavioral contract. The existing material does not provide such a contract, so we cannot assume in advance that session state is an appropriate place to carry it.

**Persistent setting.** Make whether to restore the position a long-term user preference. This is more intuitive on the settings page, but changes the nature of the question: a choice originally specific to one restore scenario would override other scenarios. Unless we can list the restore entry points that share this preference, a persistent setting is not the default candidate.

The current inclination is to validate request-level intent first. "Inclination" here does not mean a requirement to add a field immediately, but a requirement to first locate the actual construction point, message-passing points, and final point of use of the restore request in the call chain containing `tgs.js`. If these points cannot form a verifiable chain, stop at an interface draft for now rather than using a global option as a substitute.

The default behavior must remain that of the existing restore path. opt-out takes effect only when the caller explicitly expresses it; when it is not expressed, missing parameters, object deserialization, or message compatibility must not silently turn that absence into a choice not to restore the position. This requirement is not intended to attach new semantics to old entry points, but to ensure that the new choice does not also alter unmodified entry points.

We must also distinguish "no saved position" from "explicitly not using the saved position". The former is insufficient state, so the restore flow can only continue using its existing fallback behavior; the latter is a choice made by the caller. If both cases are collapsed into the same null value in transit, investigation cannot tell whether the page has no position or the position was intentionally ignored. The interface shape can be decided later, but these two states should not be confused.

## Ordering Should Not Borrow Restore State

There are also three candidate approaches for settings ordering, and they do not need to depend on whether the opt-out described above is implemented.

One approach is to retain the order in which settings declarations appear. It is intuitive, and existing entries are unlikely to drift; the downside is that when new entries are inserted later, their code location directly determines their order in the product, and reviewers must infer the UI impact from the source-file order every time.

The second approach is to provide explicit ordering criteria for entries that need to participate in sorting; when the criteria are equal or not provided, preserve the original relative order. This encodes "stability" in the rule, and the placement of new entries can also be reviewed. The cost is having to determine whether these criteria belong in the settings definitions, the rendering layer, or a centralized table; this cannot be determined solely from the current file's neighbors.

The third approach is to order entries dynamically based on runtime state, for example by moving currently available or currently relevant entries to the front. This may make short-term operations more convenient, but turns the list order into a display of state. For "Stable Ordering of Related suspend Settings", this is the riskiest approach: a change users see after an operation may not be a change in the settings' contents, but merely a state change. Unless a specific scenario explicitly requires a dynamic display, including it in this round is not recommended.

We recommend focusing the review on the second approach, with the first as a low-change fallback. Both require an explicit description up front of how tied entries are handled. Stable sorting is not merely about making a single render look good, but requires that existing entries not swap positions because of unrelated differences in input when the ordering criteria have not changed. If declaration order is ultimately retained, "where new entries are inserted and which existing entries they must not move past" should also be written as specific review checks, rather than relying on readers to remember the current file layout.

Do not bind the ordering criteria directly to display text. Copy edits, translation changes, or renaming purely for readability should not inadvertently change the relative positions of the related suspend settings. Ordering criteria should serve the relationships among the settings themselves; the specific fields or storage location remain to be determined after verification.

## Boundaries When Reviewing Together

These two changes can share a single interface review because both require checking whether callers can distinguish their own intent and whether the changes alter the default behavior existing users see. But their commits and validation must be considered separately.

The minimum checks for restore opt-out are: when the old call form is retained, the restore flow still follows the original default; a call explicitly choosing opt-out can be recognized at the final point of use; intermediate forwarding has not turned "not provided" into "explicitly do not use". Here, we cannot simply check whether a new control appears on the settings page, because the candidate approach may not introduce a persistent setting.

The minimum checks for ordering are: repeated generation of the related suspend settings under the same set of ordering criteria does not cause their relative order to drift; adding or modifying an unrelated entry does not cause existing entries to swap positions for no reason; when the ordering criteria are explicitly changed, the resulting change can be explained by the rules. A single page screenshot should not be treated as the entire validation here either, because it cannot distinguish stable rules from incidental enumeration order.

Only if the restore proposal requires a long-term toggle on the settings page should both streams of work be evaluated together at the same UI layer. Otherwise, ordering can proceed independently, while restore opt-out continues to wait for call-chain evidence. This makes the review records more fragmented than "change the settings together", but avoids packing as-yet-undetermined restore semantics into an apparently tidy bundle of options.

## Changes from Subsequent Review

MSR-213 provides a navigation entry point for Page Scroll Position Restoration opt-out. In subsequent records, that card was first marked baseline and then reassigned to its actual maintainer; the public follow-up note explicitly says not to close it because one point remains unconfirmed and specific input is missing, so it is not moving into implementation yet. This is consistent with the cautious conclusion of the initial draft, but also corrects an easy misreading: without specific input, "request-level intent" cannot be moved directly from a candidate to an interface awaiting implementation.

MSR-223 records that execution records are still missing for stable ordering of the related suspend settings. What needs to be added now is not an abstract ordering principle, but a caller still using this ordering, its actual version, the entry point used, and the current result. This gap means that the ordering proposal cannot yet select a concrete implementation layer. We can compare rules, but cannot pretend to already know which object generates the list.

The two cards are navigation points for this page, not substitutes for the trade-offs recorded here. MSR-213 must first supply the specific inputs for the restore scenario before we can determine whether opt-out is call intent or a user preference; MSR-223 must first find a caller still using the ordering before we can determine whether declaration order is sufficient or explicit criteria are needed. Neither side should be incorrectly closed because the other is not yet ready.

## Shortcuts Not Adopted

We do not recommend first adding a global "do not restore position" setting and then interpreting it as opt-out. This would quickly produce a visible toggle, but would expand a decision about a single page restore into a long-term rule for all pages. Unless caller results show that these scenarios really share the same preference, it would obscure the differences between entry points.

Nor do we recommend forcibly reordering the related suspend settings by an arbitrary fixed field before every render in the name of "stability". Fixed is not the same as stable; if the field is unrelated to the relationships among settings, users will still see existing entries move, just in a repeatable way. The ordering rules must first explain what is allowed to change positions, and why changes that are not allowed to do so will not change positions.

Finally, do not treat the currently visible imports of `tgs.js` as an implementation conclusion. `gsChrome`, `gsMascot`, `gsMessages` and `gsSession` are names of neighbors that can be followed during review, not proof of ownership of position restoration, settings ordering, or interface maintenance. If the actual call chain leaves that file, the proposal records should be revised to follow the evidence, rather than forcibly keeping responsibility here to preserve the shape of the initial draft.

## Tentative Order of Work

First fill in the specific input missing from MSR-213, and verify both the default state and the explicit opt-out state from the restore request through to the final point of use. If the results show that callers can only express a long-term preference, compare persistent settings again; if they can reliably express intent for a single operation, continue refining the compatibility path for the request-level interface.

On the ordering side, first complete the records of the caller, version, entry point, and current result for MSR-223, then choose between "declaration order" and "explicit ordering criteria with preserved relative order". Dynamic state-based ordering is not the default approach. Do not mark this proposal as an implementation decision until both branches have reviewable results.

# Troubleshooting Suspension Timeout Issues

This page starts with a very specific symptom: after the machine switches to battery power, a tab reaches its automatic suspension time but does not suspend as expected; when another tab in the same group is still active or is already background, triggering the check again may also produce different results. When troubleshooting, do not conflate "the single-tab timer has not expired" with "state changes after forced processing of the entire group". For the former, first check the timer entry point; for the latter, first check how the group state is passed in.

## Investigation Entry Point

Previous investigations have consistently led to `src/js/tgs.js`. This is not because the path name itself identifies ownership, but because `runtime`, `timeout`, `gsstorage`, `tgs`, `resetautosuspendtimerfortab`, `term`, and `alarm` in the old records all lead to this file. The direct dependencies listed at the top of the file are:

```js
import { gsChrome } from './gsChrome.js';
import { gsMascot } from './gsMascot.js';
import { gsMessages } from './gsMessages.js';
import { gsSession } from './gsSession.js';
```

For now, treat these imports as neighboring dependencies; do not use them to expand the issue into a failure of the messaging, session, or icon modules. The actionable checks currently remain within `tgs.js`: find where the single-tab timer is created, reset, and ended, then examine those separately from the group-operation entry point.

## Troubleshooting Tree

```text
Battery power + a single tab reaches timeout, but does not suspend
├─ A. Has the single-tab entry point reset the timer?
│  ├─ resetAutoSuspendTimerForTab is visible
│  │  ├─ Is term still valid?
│  │  │  ├─ Yes: continue checking whether alarm came from the same setup
│  │  │  └─ No: record where term becomes invalid, and stop counting it as a pending timer
│  │  └─ No corresponding alarm is visible: first check the completion or cleanup path
│  └─ No reset action can be found: go to B; do not infer a battery policy from the symptom
└─ B. Did this operation involve group state?
   ├─ No: keep it as a separate suspension timeout branch
   └─ Yes
      ├─ The target tab is active: record whether force applies only to other tabs in the group
      └─ The target tab is background: record whether force treats it as a tab pending processing in the group
```

### Branch A: Independent Timing

First, keep one tab fixed, do not suspend the entire group, and do not switch active/background during the check. Check whether `resetAutoSuspendTimerForTab` is called, and whether `term` and `alarm` after the call still correspond to this tab. What needs to be recorded here is the local result before and after the call: the timer was reset, the timer had already ended, or no corresponding record was found.

If you see a reset action, do not yet interpret it as "battery mode extended the duration". Battery power is only the triggering condition; what actually needs confirmation is whether this condition caused the entry point to reset the timer, or simply left an existing alarm unconsumed. If `term` has ended but `alarm` still exists, record the cleanup order; if there is no `alarm`, return to where the timer is created. In neither case should you jump to the in-group force branch.

If the single tab has not had a reset action but still has not suspended, keep the investigation focused on the code adjacent to the single-tab timer in `tgs.js`. The current records do not provide enough information to determine whether browser timing, session state, or values passed by the caller caused this, so only record observations here, without assigning responsibility to any module.

### Branch B: In-Group State

For a group operation, record two things together: whether the target tab was active or background at the time, and whether force targeted the entire group or a particular member. Do not just record "the entire group did not suspend". As long as there is one active tab in the group, the result may differ from a group whose tabs are all background; this is precisely why this page retains the term "Intra-Group active/background force Semantics", but that term cannot replace observing each tab individually.

During verification, first keep group membership unchanged. In the first round, process only one active tab, and record its state and the states of the background tabs in the same group; in the second round, leave the membership unchanged and only change the target tab to background, then check the same force entry point. Do not casually reset all tabs' timers between the two rounds, or you will be unable to determine whether the difference comes from group state or a new timer.

When you see that an active tab has not suspended, do not immediately assume it blocked the entire group operation. Distinguish three outcomes: the active tab is skipped but the background tabs continue to be processed; force takes effect for all members; the entry point never receives the group state at all. Only the third outcome allows the investigation to move back to the group-operation call site. For the first two outcomes, stay in this branch for now and record the correspondence between tab states and timer entry points.

### Recovery Actions That Have Failed

Early investigations tended to rerun suspension for the entire group directly. This action has a problem: it changes member states and timers at the same time, so seeing a tab suspend afterward does not establish that the original independent timeout has recovered. Therefore, a whole-group retry can only be recorded as an observation, not used as evidence that the independent timeout passed.

Another easily confused action is to clear only the old alarm and then wait. If you have not first recorded whether `term` is still valid, an empty result after cleanup cannot distinguish between "the old timer had already ended" and "a timer that still needed to wait was just deleted". During verification, first record the local state before cleanup; if this cannot be done, stop at recording observations and do not proceed with recovery actions.

Also avoid treating `gsstorage` as the timer itself. It appears among the search terms from earlier investigations, but the current material only establishes that it is one of the entry points for looking back; it does not establish that the battery-power branch is determined by a stored value. Likewise, only factor dependencies such as `gsChrome` and `gsSession` into the assessment when their actual calls are visible.

## Changes from Follow-up Verification

The record dated 9 29 shows that the rollback action had already been checked; on 9 30, the implementation entered review through an existing branch. By 10 2, there was still a reminder on MSR-214 that "Independent Suspend timeout on Battery Power still has one unconfirmed point". This changed how the troubleshooting tree is closed out: a single-tab timeout cannot be considered verified just because a whole-group retry succeeds; it must retain a separate branch.

Therefore, [MSR-214] is now used as the entry point for revisiting single-tab timeout, while [MSR-216] is reserved for routine checks of in-group active/background force. These two cards are not two titles for the same reproduction steps: the former needs the single-tab user flow added, while the latter needs checks based on group state; continue to leave gaps where evidence is missing.

## On-Call Record Format

For each verification, record at least the following local values; there is no need to copy the entire execution sequence:

- Whether the machine is on battery power;
- Whether the target tab is being handled by a single-tab operation or a group operation;
- The active/background states of the target tab and the other tabs in the same group;
- Whether `resetAutoSuspendTimerForTab` appears;
- The relationship between `term` and `alarm` after creation, reset, and cleanup;
- Whether the final outcome is suspension, remaining active, or insufficient information to determine the outcome.

If the single-tab branch reproduces, continue investigating along the local sequence of `term` / `alarm`; if only the group operation reproduces, record the member states before checking the force entry point. If neither branch can be reproduced reliably, record only the environment and the observed states, and do not present "not reproduced" as meaning that the semantics have been established.

The initial draft placed focus Event trailing debounce and service worker Responsiveness Recovery Routing side by side because field observations often covered the debug page, diagnostic content, and tab state at the same time. The review material contains one fairly specific gap: service worker Responsiveness Recovery Routing in the segment between the diagnostic content and the debug page is still unconfirmed, with the inputs and outputs retained in before-and-after storage snapshots. The focus and recovery tracks are therefore recorded separately.

The focus track must capture the order of consecutive focus events and retain the result on the page after the trailing phase. Successful and failed calls need the same observation point to show whether their final results are comparable. If the page is still in its old state when a call fails, the record cannot just say "no change"; it must also include whether there were adjacent focus events beforehand and whether the debug page or storage changed at the same time. The focus track only answers what remains on the page after the consecutive events have settled; new content on the diagnostic page is not a substitute for the event order.

The recovery track separately retains diagnostic content, debug page content, and before-and-after storage snapshots. All three are kept in the same set of samples to see whether they appear in the same observed case, not to treat any one of them as proof that recovery is complete. If diagnostic content changes but the debug page does not update along with it, or the debug page changes but responsiveness is still unconfirmed, record that as is. If storage already shows a difference but the page side is unchanged, do not infer backwards that any particular segment has completed; the material only shows that these points were not observed in the same way.

Two approaches were compared at the time. One was to have focus coalescing and the recovery action share a deferral point. That would make field records shorter, but after a failure it would be hard to tell which part showed a discrepancy: focus, response, page refresh, or storage state. The other was to retain two assessment points and save their respective results side by side in the same field sample. The latter is the approach adopted at this stage.

A shared deferral point is appealing because it allows just one final page state to be retained. That is also the problem: if the page changes after consecutive focus events, the person recording it will tend to log that change as recovery; if the page does not change, focus coalescing, missing diagnostic content, and storage state not being in sync get lumped into the same failure category. Separating the assessment points does not fill in the implementation chain, but it at least lets the samples retain where the difference occurred.

If a segment of the recovery track is unconfirmed, the focus track can still retain its own results as observed; the reverse also holds.
