# History of Focus and Recovery Routing

This record originally put two terms that often appeared together on the same page: focus Event trailing debounce, and service worker Responsiveness Recovery Routing. Both had been mentioned in connection with debug pages, diagnostic content, and tab state, so the first draft used a single "final state after a delay" to describe both. That wording read smoothly, but collapsed two different questions into one: when the page changed later, was it because consecutive focus events had been coalesced, because the service worker had resumed responding, or simply because the page had read the content later.

There is still one working practice from the old draft worth keeping: do not keep only images showing success. There must be samples of both successful and failed calls for consecutive events. What really needs to change is the practice of treating any page refresh as a conclusion for both. Focus events and recovery routing can occur next to each other during the same operation, and the record must first separate them before discussing whether there is a connection. The latest field feedback also provided no material that could link the two into a single execution path, so the change here is to the assessment approach, rather than forcing a new implementation attribution onto the old entry point.

Early searches started at `src/js/debug.js`. It is a nearby entry point commonly used for debugging and checking historical behavior, and the direct dependencies at the top of the file are as follows:

```js
import { gsBackup } from './gsBackup.js';
import { gsChrome } from './gsChrome.js';
import { gsFavicon } from './gsFavicon.js';
import { gsIndexedDb } from './gsIndexedDb.js';
```

These four names served a practical purpose in the old record: they kept searches from focusing only on the word focus, and reminded readers that the debugging area also sits alongside backup, browser, icon, and indexed database objects. But an import list is not a recovery path diagram. In particular, the presence of `gsIndexedDb` here does not mean that every pair of before-and-after storage snapshots can be interpreted as output from the recovery route; similarly, the presence of `gsChrome` or `gsFavicon` is not enough to show that a particular focus event has undergone specific processing.

When starting a search from this file, focus, debug, timer, event, tab, info, and query remain useful local search terms. They point to the debugging-side scope where earlier investigations had paused, not a call chain that can be followed from beginning to end. For the focus track, first look at consecutive events and page results; for the recovery track, first look at diagnostic content, debug pages, and before-and-after storage states. The objects differ, so the points to revisit also differ. Presenting an import name or search term as proof for either track would bring back the confusion in the first draft.

The initial assessment treated "trailing" as a generic moment during field observation: after consecutive focus events arrived, observe the page after the last event; when the service worker was temporarily unresponsive, revisit the debug page at roughly the same time. This assessment did not specify a wait duration, did not define new event priorities, and did not connect recovery actions to the tab state machine. It only tried to give the field material a common observation point.

The common observation point later became a source of misleading conclusions. It made recorders likely to write only "the page eventually looked normal" or "the page did not change," without noting how many focus events actually occurred in between or specifying where the respective changes in the diagnostic content, debug page, and storage landed. As a result, focus-merging failure, a service worker thread failing to respond in time, delayed appearance of diagnostic content, and the page itself not yet being refreshed could all be recorded as the same phenomenon. The old draft folded these distinctions into a single deferred action, so the shorter the sample, the harder it was to know which side to review next.

During review, no material emerged that could combine the two tracks into a single execution path. Instead, the field materials identified a narrow but clear gap: service worker Responsiveness Recovery Routing still had one unconfirmed point between the diagnostic content and the debug page, with the input and output preserved in before-and-after storage snapshots. This is not a complete implementation attribution, nor does it indicate which import module the unconfirmed section belongs to; it indicates that the earlier page assessment was too hasty.

When the diagnostic content has changed but the debug page has not, this page does not supply an answer for this evidence as to whether the missing piece on the page side is the read result or the recovery process. When new content appears on the debug page but service worker thread responsiveness has not yet been confirmed, the page change is recorded only as a page change. When storage shows a before-and-after difference, what is recorded is the state of the input and output before and after they pass through storage; the difference itself does not automatically record recovery as complete. The three types of material may occur in sequence, or may temporarily fail to line up; the current record does not justify turning this desynchronization into a consistent success conclusion.

These revisions change not "the need to look at the debugging materials," but the division of labor among the materials. Diagnostic content answers what the diagnostic chain left behind; the debug page answers what the page side read; before-and-after storage snapshots preserve the before-and-after states of the input and output. All three can appear simultaneously in one sample, or can be out of sync with one another. They are placed together for comparison, not as three duplicate proofs of success.

At the time, two recording approaches were actually compared.

The first was a shared deferred point. The merging of consecutive focus events and the recovery action both captured the final state at the same deferred point. The field notes were shorter, and it was also easier to compress a set of page changes into a single result. This approach retained the convenience of the original idea that "if things happen in the same session, record them together": one person only needed to inspect the page once after the operation ended, then append the changes on the debug side alongside it. For scenarios without failure samples, it appeared sufficient.

The cost showed up in failure samples. When the page did not reach the expected state, a single result could not determine whether to revisit the ordering of events, the service worker thread's response, the diagnostic content refresh, or the before-and-after state of storage. More troublesome, a changed page could also obscure the unconfirmed section: consecutive focus events may already have settled, and the page may already have read the content, while the diagnostic content and debug page along the recovery path still do not line up. The shared deferred point would write this kind of observation down as "already recovered," making it impossible in the next round to identify the gap that had originally been left open.

The second option is not to share evaluation points. The focus track retains consecutive events and the page result after trailing; the recovery track retains diagnostic content, the debug page, and before-and-after storage snapshots. The two tracks can reference the same operation, but each must provide its own observation point. This option retains some extra material, but it keeps failed samples useful: when the focus result has already appeared but the recovery evidence still has gaps, the former can be recorded as observed without forcing closure on the latter; when recovery-related output appears first and a new focus arrives afterward, the new event will not be retroactively treated as the cause of the earlier output.

This page adopts the second option. The reason is not that the two can never occur together, but that they require different counterexamples. A counterexample for the focus track is that consecutive focus events have arrived, but the page result after trailing does not match the successful sample. A counterexample for the recovery track is that the page or logs have changed, but the service worker's responsiveness still cannot be confirmed. If only the shared deferred action is retained, both types of counterexample will be compressed into a vague "anomaly".

This decision only addresses how records are captured on this page. It does not specify exact wait values or introduce new event priorities; it does not define recovery actions as part of the tab state machine; nor does it declare that a particular import in `src/js/debug.js` is where recovery routing is implemented. These points are left open because the existing material is only sufficient to compare observation points, not to draw conclusions about implementation relationships. The decision itself is: the two tracks will no longer share a single final page state as the basis for evaluation.

## What to Retain for the Focus Track

The focus track starts with event order. focus Event trailing debounce here means: after consecutive focus events arrive, use the trailing phase as the checkpoint for the page result of the current round. It is not a rule to "wait every time the page changes", nor does it define a new processing order for other events. Here, trailing serves only to place the observation point for the same sequence of consecutive focus events after the last event.

At a minimum, a sample should show whether there were any further adjacent focus events before the final page result. For successful calls, retain the visible differences on the page before and after the call, and indicate that the observation took place after the trailing phase. For failed calls, retain the result at the same point. This ensures that the comparison is between observations of the same kind, rather than between a process record and a final screenshot. If a successful sample contains only the final page, it still lacks the context needed to determine whether consecutive events were coalesced; if a failed sample contains only the "old state", it likewise cannot be compared with the successful sample.

If the page in a failed sample remains in the old state, do not stop at a single statement that there was "no change". The old state may appear after consecutive focus events, or it may be accompanied by debug page updates, delayed diagnostic content, or storage changes. The material does not need to assign responsibility for every possibility here, but it must retain the objects that appeared during the same operation and their chronological relationships. The focus track's conclusions concern only the page result after event coalescing, without using material from the recovery track as a substitute.

This track has an easily overlooked boundary: the page looking normal in the end does not automatically mean that every intermediate focus event had its own result. What is observed here is the result left on the page after the sequence of events has settled, not event-by-event confirmation. Conversely, if the page is still unchanged at the end, that does not mean that none of the preceding focus events were processed. Samples should preserve the relationships between consecutive events precisely to avoid inferring a separate attribution for each event from the page's final state.

Another easily confused scenario is this: consecutive focus events have been coalesced as expected, and the page looks normal in the end, while the recovery-related evidence still has an unconfirmed segment between the diagnostic content and the debug page. At this point, the focus track can complete its own record, while the recovery track continues to leave the gap open; describing the entire operation as "successful recovery" would lose the part that remains unconfirmed. The fact that the focus results are now comparable means only that the focus results are now comparable, not that the recovery track can be closed out early.

MSR-220 are retained as navigation for the current focus-event entry point and result checks. This card requires recording the visible results for focus Event trailing debounce in one successful call and one failed call, respectively. For this card, the most useful evidence is not a single image of the final page, but a record showing the relationship between consecutive focus events, the state after trailing, and the call results. If the same operation also includes diagnostic content or changes to storage, these can be retained as parallel observations, but should not be recast as substitute evidence for whether focus coalescing worked.

## Preserving the recovery track

The recovery track starts with service worker Responsiveness Recovery Routing. It does not use a single refresh of the debug page as the endpoint for assessment, but instead saves the diagnostic content, debug page content, and before-and-after storage snapshots side by side. The diagnostic content is used to review what the diagnostic flow left behind; the debug page is used to see the content actually read on the page side; the snapshots are used to preserve the state of inputs and outputs as they pass through storage. When all three appear in the same operation, their relative order should be preserved, rather than selecting only the one that looks most like "success".

The diagnostic content and the debug page are not the same observation surface. A change in the former only shows that new content was left on the diagnostic side; a change in the latter only shows that the page side read content. Even simultaneous changes in both can only serve as part of the evidence from the same operation, and do not automatically provide the missing assessment of service worker responsiveness. Writing them up separately is intended to keep "there is still an unconfirmed point in between" visible, rather than hide the gap in a blanket recovery record.

The before-and-after storage snapshots should not be treated as an additional final state either. The value of the snapshots is that they preserve what the inputs and outputs look like on either side of storage, so that a later review can identify where a particular change occurred. They can help identify what else is present before and after changes to the diagnostic content or debug page, but they are not an independent marker that the recovery route has completed. If the snapshots differ while the other two observation points are not in sync, the record should preserve that inconsistency; if the other two observation points have changed but the snapshots have no comparable content, do not invent a cause to fill the gap.

Another counterexample is when recovery-related output has already appeared, followed by a new focus event. The new focus changes when the page is subsequently observed, but does not automatically become the cause of the earlier recovery output. When recording this, keep the earlier output on the recovery track and the page result after the new trailing phase on the focus track. If consistent ordering constraints emerge later, a separate decision can be made; currently, there is no evidence to describe the two as sharing a timer or belonging to the same execution chain.

Nor can an inventory of the current build configuration replace the recovery track. Configuration materials answer where the platforms and versions relevant to dependents should be recorded; evidence from the observed session answers what the response process left behind. Even if the configuration items have been organized, that does not eliminate the unconfirmed parts between the diagnostic content and the debug page. Conversely, if the session samples are complete but the dependents have not yet been inventoried, the samples cannot be interpreted as complete platform coverage.

MSR-221 is retained as a navigation aid for service worker Responsiveness Recovery Routing's current inventory of dependents. The platforms and versions involved in the current build configuration still need to be mapped to specific configuration files. This card is adjacent to the debug entry point, but they are not the same task: the configuration inventory captures the scope of dependencies, while the diagnostic content, debug page, and before-and-after storage snapshots preserve the before-and-after states from a single observed session. Both sides must continue, and neither can finish the work on behalf of the other.

## Scope of use for the old entry point

When you need to look back through older records, you can start with names such as focus, debug, timer, event, tab, info, and query near `src/js/debug.js`. This entry point helps locate objects on the debugging side, rather than drawing conclusions on behalf of the session samples. When you encounter a storage change, first check whether it is input or the state before and after output; when you encounter a debug page change, first check what the page side actually read; when you encounter consecutive focus events, first check the page result after trailing. The lookup order is determined by the object being checked, not by the imported name.

The presence of `gsBackup`, `gsChrome`, `gsFavicon`, and `gsIndexedDb` together in the file header is retained as a reminder to readers: the debug file does not serve only a single focus event. If an older investigation leads here from a particular issue name or call name, readers still need to return to the actual references to identify the relationships. The current decision does not include backup, browser, icon, or IndexedDB objects in the success criteria for the focus track, nor does it require the recovery track to pass through each of them.

Therefore, the old draft's use of "deferral" as a shared shorthand for both tracks is no longer retained. It is retained only on the focus track: the trailing phase of focus Event trailing debounce is where the page result is checked. The recovery track does not use this point as a substitute for assessing responsiveness, but instead continues to check whether the diagnostic content, debug page, and before-and-after storage snapshots align with one another. This correction does not deny that the two tracks can appear in the same observed session, but simply no longer allows them to validate each other using the same final page state.

The diagram below shows only how records are separated into tracks on this page, does not show the execution order, and does not indicate that the two tracks share any state:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "focus event" as FocusEvent
    state "trailing debounce" as TrailingDebounce
    state "Page result" as PageResult
    state "service worker Responsiveness Recovery Routing" as RecoveryRoute
    state "Diagnostic content" as DiagnosticData
    state "Debug page" as DebugPage
    state "Before-and-after storage snapshots" as StorageSnapshots

    [*] --> FocusEvent
    FocusEvent --> TrailingDebounce
    TrailingDebounce --> PageResult
    [*] --> RecoveryRoute
    RecoveryRoute --> DiagnosticData
    RecoveryRoute --> DebugPage
    RecoveryRoute --> StorageSnapshots
```

The two starting points in the diagram indicate that the subjects should first be considered separately when reading it. The focus flow runs from consecutive events to the page result after trailing; the recovery flow runs from the recovery route to three types of captured evidence. The two flows may appear in the same set of samples, but each retains its own results. Without confirmation of a shared timing reference, no additional merged state is drawn, and the diagram's relationships do not imply that one piece of evidence necessarily precedes another.

Two types of evidence are still missing. The focus flow lacks failed-call results that can be compared with successful calls, particularly how consecutive focus events relate to one another and the page state after trailing. The recovery flow lacks evidence from the same input instance that allows direct comparison of the diagnostic content, debug page content, and before-and-after storage snapshots; the existing records only indicate that the point of uncertainty lies between the diagnostic content and the debug page. How to display another focus event occurring while recovery is still unconfirmed has also not yet been decided, so for now the two flows are kept separate, rather than collapsed into a single final result.

The decision for this round ends here: focus Event trailing debounce will check the page results for the trailing phase; service worker Responsiveness Recovery Routing will independently verify them using the diagnostic content, debug page, and before-and-after storage snapshots. Appearing next to each other does not constitute mutual corroboration, and the missing segment will remain a gap.

- Check whether the link target provides a revision;

# Tracing revisions from the img entry point

This page has been used as the entry-point guide for img · Dependency Boundary Audit, but its starting point is itself a page that changes, not a fixed export. The path is still `docs/adj-img/notes/from-current-entry-point-to-current-revision.md`. The latest-known beside the path only indicates that this was the knowledge-base export visible at the time; the body and attachments are still maintained by the adj-img project. What follows therefore preserves a route from the public entry point back to `img-supply-boundary`, not a final listing for any particular revision.

The earliest note was brief: found the entry point, then tried to follow it further. At the time, treating "current" as a navigation hint was fine, but it later became easy to read it as "the current page already represents the only version." That working assumption from the old notes is retained here: the entry-point name can be a clue for finding the first destination; it was never a basis for establishing provenance.

When tracing back now, first write down four things separately on paper. The first is the text displayed at the public entry point; the second is the `img-supply-boundary` it actually points to; the third is the revision included in the link; the fourth, finally, is the source that can be reached by tracing that revision back. The first two often appear together, so they are the easiest to copy onto the same line; if either of the latter two is missing, the trace can only be marked incomplete.

The first fork at the entry point usually doesn't need to be expanded into a string of module names. If a link leads to an object with a revision, follow it back; if there is only an adjacent display item with the same name and no link relationship, leave it beside the entry point. Don't infer that lock and license share a dependency source just because they appear in the same set of notes. What they describe here is the provenance, adoption scope, and exit responsibilities covered by the dependency-boundary audit, not call order.

The change added later to the second version still applies: separate by revision first, then determine provenance. `MSRA-018` points toward following the revision of `img-supply-boundary` back to the earliest reconstructable source, rather than inferring it from the display text. This requirement changed how to read the old page; it did not add a direct call edge that hadn't existed before.

`MSRA-023` recorded a mixed display of old and new `img-supply-boundary`. When you encounter an entry point like this, first write down each link's revision: keep the old link with its old destination and put the new link on a separate line. Even if the two records have exactly the same name, don't merge them into one "newer" object. Someone previously kept only the display name, and later it was no longer possible to tell which one it pointed to; that's exactly why this page is still worth keeping.

One passage in the old wording needs its limits made explicit. The first version listed "keep looking for the direct caller" as the next step, as though a caller were a required stop between the entry point and the revision. In hindsight, that requirement was too strong: this page has no record of that call edge, and there is no need to guess one just to complete the path. If the relationship between the entry link, object, and revision can be confirmed, recording the trace back to the source is enough; include the caller in that same chain only if a specific revision has already supplied a direct caller.

Side notes on temporary maintenance should not be mixed into provenance judgments either. `MSRA-013` left an action item to confirm who will take over before the temporary owner's assignment expires; if no one takes over, leave the slot vacant. It can help readers understand why part of the record has no follow-up additions, but it cannot establish that the object corresponding to the vacant slot has no source, much less identify the temporary maintainer as the person responsible for exit.

This page stops earlier than the old draft:

1. Get the link target from the public entry point;
2. Separate the target from the display item with the same name;
3. If there is a revision, trace it back to the earliest reconstructable source;
4. If there is no revision, or old and new links are mixed together, preserve the forks and stop.

Do not cross into the main project's internal implementation. img is only responsible for dependency sources associated with lock and license, along with the related adoption scope and exit responsibilities; implementation details in the shared product are outside this trace. `DOC-26` can serve as an entry point to records for part of the same audit project, but it won't fill in an edge that wasn't recorded for this page.

The direct caller is still unresolved. The export path can locate the entry page, but it cannot prove who calls in from outside the page; the attachments aren't included in this export either. If a call relationship can later be obtained from a specific revision, it should be added under the branch for that revision, rather than backfilled as "the current entry point has always been this way." Until then, retaining the facts while keeping the path, object name, and two versions separate is already more reliable than stitching similar names together.

# img Dependency Boundary State Review

The anomaly concerns not a single piece of artwork, but the dependency source defined by lock and license, along with its scope of adoption, maintenance arrangements, and exit responsibilities. It has its own schedule, maintainer, and exit criteria. During the incident window, the debug page probe showed content that did not match the old record; a subsequent review of the current entry point also found different current revision values at two points in time. It was unclear at the time which value could represent the full state, so the later value was not used to overwrite the earlier record.

The original record and the recovery page were retained as two separate artifacts. The former preserves the state first observed; the latter preserves the state available for review during recovery. The difference between them is itself part of the incident. The entry page was treated only as the entry point visible at the time, not as the sole basis for replacing the original record. No confirmed explanation was available for the changes to the older artwork, and no speculation was entered in the cause field.

## Timeline

- **7/15 incident window**: The debug page probe first failed to match the old record. Further checks of the current entry point found that it returned different current revision values at two points in time. The early records did not explain why these values differed or provide enough evidence to order them.
- **Investigation during the incident**: At one point, someone attributed the discrepancy to a "persistence race." This assessment had no supporting reproduction artifacts and could not explain why the original record, recovery page, and entry page each contained different content. Continuing to retry would keep creating new states, so retries were stopped.
- **Recovery assessment**: The dependency lock file could be restored, and the recovery action was recorded separately on the recovery page. The original record was not deleted, and the recovered content was not backfilled as the state at the time of the incident. Speculation that adjacent services might have been involved was not included in the causal attribution.
- **7/27 release window**: The review used only the saved lock file, original record, and recovery page. During the release window, the values displayed later on the entry page were not retroactively treated as the incident state on 7/15; why the older artwork changed remained unconfirmed.

## Impact boundaries

This discrepancy primarily affects the assessment of the dependency source. The scope of adoption cannot be determined solely from the current revision shown by the entry page on any one occasion, because that would ignore the existing divergence between the original record and the recovery page. Exit actions also cannot be expanded on the basis of this recovery: the lock file's ability to restore the dependency source does not mean no one still uses the item, much less that the associated exit responsibilities can be removed.

The maintainer and independent schedule remained in place during the incident, but they cannot fill in the missing information about users. The teams still using adj-img have not yet been confirmed, and this record does not verify who made the last confirmation or who is responsible for exports. Therefore, "no one uses it" is not grounds for cleanup. If later work involves exit actions, the last access and export responsibilities need to be traced first; if non-use cannot be established, retain the original scope.

## Withdrawn attribution

"Persistence race" is retained as a working hypothesis from the time, not as the cause of this anomaly. It did not explain the current revision values at the two points in time, nor could it connect the changes in the older artwork to the lock file. Only three things could later be confirmed: the debug page probe differed from the old record; the entry point returned different values at different times; and the lock file provided a usable recovery path.

Successful recovery must not be recast as proof that the cause has been identified. The lock file shows that the dependency source can be returned to its saved state, but it does not prove that the older artwork changed because of the lock file, much less that all adopters have migrated away. The original record, the recovery page, and the unresolved status of the cause must all be preserved together; otherwise, the next review will show only the last recovery result, with no way to identify the divergence present during the incident.

## Follow-up review

The next time an entry point value does not match the record, first compare the original record, the recovery page, and the current revision shown by the entry point at that time side by side, then decide whether recovery is needed. Do not use only the last displayed value or overwrite an old page with new entry point content. Continue to handle the dependency source associated with lock and license within the boundaries of adj-img; do not fill in the scope of adoption or exit criteria based on speculation about adjacent services.

For investigation entry points for the same dependency boundary, see DOC-27. This page records the discrepancies observed during this anomaly, the decision to stop retrying, and the lock file recovery result, not unconfirmed failure mechanisms.

Still unconfirmed: why the older artwork changed; why the current entry point returned different current revision values at two points in time; which teams still use adj-img, who made the last confirmation, and who is responsible for exports.

# js Release Automation User FAQ

This page covers only the few entry-point questions that users keep asking. The context is the build queue formed by `.github/workflows`, as well as artifact versions and the rollback window; these items have separate scheduling, a maintainer, and exit criteria in js · Release Automation.

### Where is the current entry point?

Start with `docs/adj-js/faq/js-release-automation-three-consumer-questions.md`. It is the export entry point for the js · Release Automation knowledge base, and the related body and attachments are still maintained by that project. This page already records two locations: `Drive backup` and `Settings page options`. When checking either one, first confirm which section you are looking at; do not treat results from the administrator side or an internal environment directly as an answer for regular users.

The section originally reserved after `Release notes` is still incomplete. The earlier Drive backup content cannot be used in its place, and this version of the FAQ does not add new wording for it.

### What does "current revision" mean here?

This page corresponds to that knowledge base's `latest-known` export. `latest-known` is a status label left in the page navigation, not a repository commit ID that can be verified from this version's body. The page does not preserve a more specific current revision, so the export page alone cannot determine which commit the build queue actually uses, nor can a value seen on a settings page be recorded as the project's fixed version.

If the question concerns an artifact version, first keep the artifact name and page location seen by the user in place, then return to the project's maintained attachments to verify them. Without these two items, this page has no conclusion.

### Where do we pick up after the build gets stuck?

First, follow the project page above and its attachments to reach js · Release Automation's maintenance entry point. This version has not recorded a verifiable person's name, message channel, or alternative entry point, so this page cannot infer "who to hand it off to." What can be confirmed is that the project has its own maintainer and exit criteria; they do not constitute the main project's handling commitment.

When taking over, retain at least these three pieces of context as seen by the user: the entry point, artifact version, and rollback window. If you only know that the queue is stuck but do not know the corresponding artifact or rollback window, continue asking follow-up questions; do not fill in the gaps with the handling result from a neighboring project.

### What other questions are still unanswered?

There are. Beyond the current entry point, current revision, and handoff entry point, this page draws no conclusions about the gap in the release notes, differences in the administrator environment, or future implementation. If answers are added later, leave the old assessment and new result side by side rather than overwriting the existing record in this version.

Use this when the current entry point appears stuck and it's still unclear whether js-release-automation itself, the exit action, or permissions are blocking the request.

# js release automation handoff troubleshooting

This page originally only addressed "do we need to contact the permissions owner?" During a later review, the build queue, artifact withdrawal, and the shared test environment got mixed together, and the original two-way decision was no longer enough. The tree below still starts at the existing entry point, but spells out what to retain at each step.

```text
Entry request did not complete
├─ Missing request or run id
│  └─ Get the original record; do not assign a root cause
├─ Has request/run id, but has not entered .github/workflows
│  ├─ Standard identity was rejected at the entry point
│  │  └─ Hand off to the permissions owner; include where it was rejected
│  └─ No rejection at the entry point, but still no workflow
│     └─ Stop between the entry point and workflow; wait for new records
└─ Has entered .github/workflows
   ├─ Build queue has not picked it up
   │  └─ Leave with the person on duty for js-release-automation
   └─ Queue has picked it up
      ├─ worker has not produced an artifact
      │  └─ Record run id, commit, and cache key
      └─ Artifact exists, but the exit action is not as expected
         └─ Cross-check the artifact version and withdrawal window; hand off to the permissions owner only if permissions need to change
```

"Has not entered the workflow" does not mean "it must be a permissions issue." When a standard identity is rejected at the entry point, the rejection location and request/run id are the evidence to send to the permissions side; if there is no rejection at the entry point but no workflow appears, this page goes no further than the gap between the two. Do not treat old config in the directory, the last green run, or another execution of the same commit as evidence that the handoff went through.

Once in `.github/workflows`, the original run matters more than a rerun. First copy down the run id, commit, cache key, and artifact version. If a recent good sample is available, compare only the first point of divergence: whether the queue picked it up, whether the worker started, or whether the exit action changed the subsequent state. Do not change the account, commit, and cache key at the same time in one comparison; that would mix entry-point issues and cache issues together.

The old version simply said to handle it within the project once "the queue has picked it up." That was convenient but too coarse. If the worker has no artifact, still keep it in js-release-automation to start with: just record where the run got to between the queue and the worker; do not assume it is a platform issue based on how long it has been waiting. Hand it off only when a permissions change is confirmed to be necessary, or the exit action has already gone beyond what the project can handle. Here, "handoff" does not mean clearing out the failed sample; it means passing along the same request, run id, and first visible state.

When the shared test environment is unavailable, a non-author reviewer cannot sign off based on the original author's green result. MSRB-005 was once blocked for this reason, then returned to the backlog because it missed the release window. That record remains here: it shows that "wait for the environment to recover, then rerun" was what actually happened, not that the rerun result can stand in for the original state.

Another complication was documented later: the same person on duty can specify different expiry actions on the two sides. When that happens, do not decide here which action takes priority; leave the commands and exit codes side by side for the person taking over, and label each with its corresponding request. If either the command or the exit code is missing, write down only the entry-point state you have seen; do not invent the intermediate steps.

Stop conditions:

- No original request or run id: stop at evidence collection; do not discuss the queue, worker, or permissions.
- Standard identity explicitly rejected at the entry point: hand off to the permissions owner; do not also change the build config.
- workflow has appeared but the queue has not picked it up: leave it in js-release-automation.
- Both the queue and worker have appeared, but there is no artifact: retain the commit, cache key, and run id, and leave further assessment to the person on duty for the project.
- An artifact is present and action is required within the withdrawal window: first confirm whether the exit action is irreversible; if that is unclear, do not step in to execute it.

When taking over, use `docs/adj-js/runbooks/js-release-automation-blocked-escalation-contacts.md` to open this page as before. MSRB-004 can serve as a navigation aid for rejections at the standard entry point; it is not a blanket explanation for every stall.

# js Release Automation Handoff Troubleshooting

This tree originally focused only on entry-point denials, so it still contains quite a bit of permissions-oriented wording. Several later handoffs showed that the actual blockage is often after the entry point: the request already exists, and `.github/workflows` may also be present, but the build queue, worker, artifacts, and rollback actions are not all part of the same processing stage. The old tree has not been deleted, so it is easier to see why issues were handed off too early at the time; the notes below do not turn it into the current release manual either.

First, obtain original records from the current entry point that can be reviewed later. There should be at least a request or a run id; if neither is available, the only option is to collect the missing records. Screenshots, verbal descriptions, and a green result after a rerun cannot fill this slot. When access with a regular user identity fails, record where the denial occurred at the entry point before deciding whether to involve the permissions side. MSRB-004 remain as navigation cards for this type of entry-point failure.

The first tree in the old version:

```text
Blocked at the current entry point
├─ No original records: collect the missing records
└─ Original records available
   ├─ Has not entered the build queue: hand off to the permissions owner
   └─ Has entered the build queue: find the js-release-automation on-call person
```

This tree is no longer accurate enough, but it has not been deleted. It incorrectly turned "the queue was not seen" into "the entry point definitely needs permissions handling." In actual troubleshooting, if the entry point did not deny access but no workflow appeared, that only shows that the records stop between the two stages; it is neither a conclusion about permissions nor grounds for asking worker to take over. The old tree is still useful when handoffs are busy: it reminds people to find the original records first, rather than first finding an owner who seems relevant.

### First, check what the entry point left behind

When the current entry point has returned a denial, retain the request, run id (if one has been generated), and denial location. A denial for a regular user identity should go to the permissions owner; do not switch to an administrator identity to verify permissions and then declare that the issue has disappeared. An administrator getting through only shows that the administrator is taking a different path, not that the regular-user entry point has recovered.

When the current entry point has not explicitly denied access, but there is no request or run id, first add the last verifiable state before the failure. MSRB-011 document exactly this gap. The goal of adding records is not to complete a polished timeline, but to let the person taking over know on which side the request disappeared. Without this record, all subsequent judgments about `.github/workflows`, the build queue, and worker should stop.

Only after the entry point has provided a request or run id should you check `.github/workflows`. Ask just one question here: does this request have a corresponding run record. Do not infer that it has entered workflow from other runs of the same commit, artifacts with the same name, or an old cached page. If there is no corresponding record, attach the existing request and entry-point status, and stop at the connection between the entry point and workflow; if there is a corresponding record, continue downstream using the run id.

```text
request or run id obtained
├─ No corresponding workflow found
│  ├─ Entry point explicitly denied a regular user identity → permissions owner
│  └─ Entry point did not deny access             → retain records, stop between the entry point and workflow
└─ workflow found
   ├─ Queue has not picked it up              → js-release-automation on-call person
   └─ Queue has picked it up              → check worker and artifacts
```

"No corresponding workflow found" here must refer to the same request or run id. When an old page only shows the latest green run, do not treat the run on that page as the sample for this attempt. If there is only a commit and no request, first return to the entry point to collect the missing records; commit can be used as a field for later comparisons, but cannot replace the identity of this run.

### Old habits after workflow

Early on-call practice tended to start with a rerun. The reason was simple: when the rerun turned green, the build queue appeared to have recovered. This approach was later withdrawn because it overwrote the most valuable sample, the first failure. A rerun can be a separate attempt, but should come after the original run has been saved; the artifact version from the rerun must not replace the artifact version from the original run either.

When retaining a sample, use the most recent normal run as a comparison, but choose only one condition at a time. You can compare commit first, then cache key; if commit and cache key both changed, record "cannot distinguish," and do not work backward from the result to infer which one caused the queue to stall. The same applies to worker: being able to see worker records does not mean you have explained why the queue has taken so long to pick it up.

The old version said, "Once the queue has picked it up, keep it within the project." This sentence remains, but should be understood with the following boundaries: when the queue has not picked it up, that is the first point for the js-release-automation on-call person to handle; when the queue has picked it up but worker has no artifacts, the project on-call person is still responsible for retaining the run id, commit, cache key, and worker location. Handing it off without these fields will only make the recipient find the sample all over again.

```text
workflow has appeared
├─ Build queue has not picked it up
│  └─ Hand off to the js-release-automation on-call person; attach run id
└─ Build queue has picked it up
   ├─ No worker records found
   │  └─ Retain the queue location and run id, do not describe it as a permissions issue
   ├─ worker has records but no artifacts
   │  └─ Attach commit, cache key, and the location where artifacts are missing
   └─ Artifacts have appeared
      └─ Move on to exit actions and the rollback window
```

Do not merge "no worker records found" with "worker has no artifacts." The former means the records at hand have not yet reached worker, while the latter means worker has been seen but artifacts have not appeared; these two cases require different materials when handed to the project on-call person. For the former, provide the queue location and run id; for the latter, also add commit, cache key, and the location where the artifact version is missing. Do not describe it as a failure of some external system unless records about that system already exist outside this page.

Once artifacts appear, the question is no longer just whether the build succeeded. Confirm the artifact version, then check whether exit actions have begun to affect the rollback window. If the exit actions are reversible, first record the actions and version; if it is still unclear whether they are irreversible, stop here, and do not use "run it again" to verify. MSRB-018 are drill cards for using the rollback entry point with a regular user identity, suitable for opening when entry-point behavior needs to be confirmed; they do not replace retaining a specific failed run.

### Old guidance on permissions and exit actions

The old records listed "permissions owner" and "exit actions" side by side as the final exits, as though it were always possible to choose one or the other. When actually taking over, first ask how far the exit actions have progressed. If a regular user identity was denied at the entry point, hand the materials to the permissions owner; if the request, workflow, queue, and artifacts are all present, and only the choice of rollback action remains, do not explain it using the entry-point denial path.

After receiving confirmation from js · Release Automation, the handling for MSRB-012 is to change only the corresponding field, while adj-js remains in its original state. This practice remains as a handoff note: update whichever field has been confirmed; do not casually fill in unconfirmed queue, worker, or artifact statuses as "recovered." It is slower than "find an owner and finish" in the old tree, but it prevents the statuses of different runs from overwriting one another.

MSRB-005 also left records of another kind of trouble: the shared test environment was unavailable, blocking non-author review; later, it was moved back to the backlog because the release window was unsuitable. When the same on-call person specified different deadline actions on the two sides, the old version recommended simply choosing the earlier one. That recommendation no longer applies. Now, this page only requires saving the commands and exit codes side by side, and marking which request they belong to; if a command or exit code is missing, do not replace it with "handled."

### Build the handoff package for the branch, do not copy everything

For the entry-point denial branch, hand over only: the regular user identity, denial location, request or run id, and initial failure state. The permissions owner does not need a string of unrelated speculation about worker.

For the missing-workflow branch, hand over only: evidence that the entry point did not explicitly deny access, request or run id, and the location where no corresponding workflow could be found. These two questions were written below the decision, where later readers could easily mistake them for "these will be resolved automatically in the next step." They would not. There was no supporting material at the time, so they were not written as commitments to take action.

The later published version stated the choice more firmly: keep the cache and the original environment side by side; do not rebuild the environment. That wording is still available, but it should be read together with the limitations in place at the time.

| Consideration at the time | Keep the existing environment | Rebuild the environment |
|---|---|---|
| Current entry point | Can continue to see the state after a hit | Must be re-established from a new starting point |
| States before and after the failure | Can be compared with the cache in the same place | Would first be separated by the new cleanup process |
| Scope of the conclusion | Applies only to this call path | Could easily be misread as a broader recovery conclusion |

So the second column was not selected. Not because rebuilding the environment was not an option, but because it addressed a different problem: getting an environment back, rather than preserving the original point of comparison at the current revision. The original draft stated only briefly that "a green result after cleanup cannot supersede the original environment." The full meaning is this: if a green result comes from a new environment, it shows only one result in that new environment and cannot replace the states before and after the failure in the original environment.

A counterexample involving the order of the records then emerged. In MSRC-006, the execution record was dated earlier than the current result. This record originally started from a search term, not from a confirmed module entry point. `backup-auth` first led people to `src/js/gsBackup.js`; the file's `backup`, `auth`, and `manifest` were adjacent to the target, so the early notes treated it as the first stop for tracing back. That judgment is still useful, but only up to "first stop."

How the early notes were read

The earliest short note stated the file location directly: find `src/js/gsBackup.js`, then look outward from the authentication and backup traces in the file. At the time, the actual actions were limited to two steps: inspect `manifest`, then inspect `lockfile diff`. The former was used to confirm whether the searched entry was still connected to the extension's assembly relationship; the latter was used to determine whether there were dependency-side changes around the migration of the browser-compatibility rerun entry. The short note did not provide a complete call chain, nor did it index the same-named files individually.

This section must not be rewritten into a new module description based on results seen later. The old wording that remains is: `src/js/gsBackup.js` looked like an entry point, and the file path also looked like the ownership location. A later trace-back only confirmed that it was suitable as a landing point near the entry; it did not confirm the stronger claim that "the path is the permanent ownership location." The old wording is included here because people still use it to find the file; it no longer supports a stronger conclusion.

The actual trace-back retains only this narrow path:

```text
backup-auth (the searched entry term)
        |
        v
src/js/gsBackup.js
        |
        v
One direct caller
        |
        v
The first actual consumer of the browser-compatibility rerun entry migration
```

Inspect the file itself first, then one direct caller. Do not infer a call relationship from the same filename: a file with no call edge is still only a signpost. The entry-migration assessment has a concrete endpoint only after reaching the first actual consumer; if only similarly named files with no actual links remain in between, do not connect them to the graph.

Local observations from the review

- `manifest` is suitable for the entry-point confirmation step. It can show whether the entry is still within the extension's assembly scope, but it cannot replace the call relationship.
- `lockfile diff` is suitable for tracing back dependency changes. It can help explain why the same search entry looks different at different times, but it is neither the name of the first consumer nor a call edge.
- The two terms `backup` and `auth` expand the search to the vicinity of backup and authentication. They answer "where to look first," not "who ultimately consumed the migration entry."
- If a same-named file has no call edge, retain the filename as a signpost for the time being. Treating it as the actual consumer would make this old path look longer than the scope supported by the record.

There is one point where the old draft can easily mislead. The first record wrote "the file is on this path" as "the entry belongs at this location." A later addendum separated the two: the path was a locator available during the rerun at that time, while the actual consumer of the entry migration still needs to be confirmed by following the direct caller. This correction does not delete the old sentence because it explains why the early search stopped here; it simply cannot be treated as permanent ownership anymore.

Code-reading order

1. Search from `backup-auth` to `src/js/gsBackup.js`, and first record the `manifest` relationships visible in the file.
2. Continue with only one direct caller that has an actual call edge. If the search results contain only same-named files, do not expand the path yet.
3. After the direct caller, find the first actual consumer of the browser-compatibility rerun entry migration. Focus on whether it actually consumes the entry, not on whether `backup` or `auth` also appear there.
4. Use `lockfile diff` to review the dependency changes around the migration. Attach it to the corresponding node as locator material; do not treat the diff as a caller.
5. Stop once you reach a boundary that requires another owner to answer; this record does not supply a name or ownership for that boundary.

The sentence "continue searching outward from the file" can remain in the old draft, but it must now be followed in the narrow order above. Otherwise, the manifest, lockfile, and same-named files will quickly be mixed into a seemingly complete chain.

Margin notes still in place

- `src/js/gsBackup.js` could serve as a trace-back starting point at the time; whether it still serves the same position must be rechecked against an actual call edge.
- The first actual consumer is the endpoint this record is trying to find; do not count every browser-compatibility-related file.
- The subsequent relationship owned by another owner remains outside the boundary.

This page is therefore best treated as an old entry map: enter through `backup-auth`, pass through `src/js/gsBackup.js`, and follow one direct caller to find the first actual consumer. The path on the map comes from the files at the time, `manifest`, and `lockfile diff`; the old judgment about fixed ownership has been downgraded to a historical note.

title: Diagnostic Data Retention On-Call Cheat Sheet

versions.body:
# Diagnostic Data Retention On-Call Cheat Sheet

When an on-site message about "diagnostic data retention policy update" arrives, first preserve the version, result, and state visible at that time. The on-call person is responsible only for freezing the scene and handing off the first divergence; leave the long-term determination of the retention scope to the relevant maintainer.

## Preserve the Scene First

Create the records in sequence; do not overwrite the material initially seen with content found in later follow-up checks.

1. Record the version of `backup-auth`. The version value should be kept with this on-site message; if an entry with the same name or another version is found later, start a separate record and state the order in which it appeared.
2. Save the unprocessed result. Preserve failure content, null values, and the original output order; you may append a brief note to the original, but do not leave only a summary.
3. Keep before-and-after snapshots of `storage`. The before-state must be saved before any operation that could change the record, and the after-state after the operation; the two snapshots must make their order discernible. Do not use the later snapshot to fill in the before-state.
4. When the scene involves `tab`, record the state seen at the time. If `tab` was not observed, record it as not observed; do not infer its state from the message content.

If the version, raw result, or before-state is still missing, do not reorganize the existing material or try to fill the gap with rerun results. Incomplete material can be handed off; do not use that to rewrite it as a fault that has already been pinpointed.

## Mark the First Divergence

Review the version, unprocessed result, and the two `storage` snapshots side by side in the order that can be confirmed. At handoff, point out only the earliest point of difference that can be established; do not assign the final attribution on the maintainer's behalf.

- Resulting version mismatch: retain both version values and where each appeared, then first verify whether they belong to the same incident.
- Result changes first: hand over the complete raw output and mark whether the change occurred before or after the before-state snapshot.
- A change appears between the before-and-after snapshots: leave the location of the change in the record; do not directly label it a `storage` fault.
- The material cannot establish the order: explicitly record which records are missing, retain each original, and do not reconstruct the order from memory.

## Hand Off to the Relevant Maintainer

Cross-module handoffs must include the call entry point, the before-state of the tab or storage, the browser version, the raw output, and the next explicitly assigned owner. If the call entry point has not yet been confirmed, write "entry point not confirmed"; if a before-state is missing, specify which before-state is missing, and do not substitute a post-action snapshot. After handoff, retain the originals and unconfirmed items; do not reorder the output content to make handoff easier.

## Stop Point

If it becomes necessary to expand permissions, change externally visible behavior, or have the on-call person decide the retention scope on behalf of the long-term maintainer, stop immediately. At that point, hand over the saved version, unprocessed result, before-and-after snapshots, and a description of the gaps; do not continue cleaning up the scene or add operations that would change the state as it stands.

title: Troubleshooting Acceptance Discrepancies in Legacy Artwork

versions.body:
# Investigating Acceptance Discrepancies in Legacy Artwork

When a ticket says Legacy Visual Assets has been accepted but the person taking it over cannot obtain the same result, don't treat the ticket's "Complete" as conclusive. This records the acceptance setup at the time: first locate the actual call entry point for visual-assets, then confirm which version is being compared. The old record checked the manifest first; this order is retained for reviewing the setup at the time and does not mean any manifest alone is enough to establish that the artwork is usable.

### Ask for the entry point first

- If you can identify where visual-assets is called from and state which version this acceptance targets: continue gathering the same input.
- If all you can provide is "already checked" or a result screenshot, with no entry point or version: stop here and ask the party that performed the original acceptance to provide these two items; don't rerun with a different input just to force a matching result.
- If the entry point exists but the version it points to does not match the legacy version described in the ticket: record the discrepancy on the original ticket, handle it as a version mismatch, and stop comparing the later files.

### Compare the two records for the same input

Once the input is confirmed, retrieve the manifest and lockfile diff generated by that input together. First check whether the objects listed in the manifest are the same, then whether the lockfile diff shows dependency version changes. If neither has changed but the results differ, the evidence on hand does not support attributing the issue to the visual assets themselves; retain this input and both outputs, and stop guessing.

When the manifest differs but the lockfile diff is unchanged, the original acceptance setup is more likely to have missed the call entry point or version. Return to the entry-point branch; don't record the discrepancy as a dependency issue. Conversely, when the manifest is the same but the lockfile diff has changed, record only "dependency record changed under the same input"; don't use that to assert which asset is correct.

### Once the result can be verified

Only after verification yields a consistent result should you supplement the ticket's "Complete" entry with the version and input used. If only one side has been verified, the ticket should remain pending the missing details. If a new file, another version, or clarification of who will confirm the dependency change is needed, stop the tree here; the person holding that material takes over, rather than having multiple people each rerun it once and then vote.

### Borrowed environment

Borrowing CI or a test account across teams can be used to obtain records for the same input. Record the return time on the original card; do not paste credentials in a public channel. If the borrowed environment cannot be clearly tied to this version, do not use it as a verification result.

This record does not treat "manifest consistency" as a go/no-go condition; it preserves only the troubleshooting sequence used at the time: find the entry point first, then cross-check the two records.

The tree stops at the first point where new evidence or a new owner is needed; it does not rely on repeated reruns and voting.
